newsitem.title: USA: GE labor talks yet to hit hot button topic.
newsitem.headline: GE labor talks yet to hit hot button topic.

text.p: Labor talks between General Electric Co and its unions won't get down to the most difficult issues involving job security until six days before contracts covering thousands of workers expire on June 29, said a union spokeswoman Wednesday.
The contract negotiations between the company and the Coordinated Bargaining Committee of GE Unions, which represents 46,000 GE workers in 14 unions, began May 28 at a New York City hotel.

So far, the two sides are meeting three days each week, broadly outlining their positions on the less contentious issues, such as wages, with talks on health-related issues and insurance scheduled for next week.
"The tone is similar to what we've seen in previous years. We've had a contract for the last eight times," said a GE spokemsan, "and we're still confident we'll negotiate a settlement."
"No surprises so far," agreed the union spokeswoman.

But starting June 23, the two sides break up into subcommittees and start bargaining over small tables, tackling the difficult issue of how General Electric can meet the union's demand to preserve jobs, and whether the company will remain neutral when the unions try to organize its plants.
That last issue is a sore point with Ed Fire, president of the International Union of Electrical Workers (IUE), the largest union involved in the GE talks.

He said that while management had worked closely and well with the union at some plants, such as GE's large Louisville, Ky., factory, where it makes major appliances, it has fought union representation bitterly at unorganized GE facilities like its refrigerator plant in Decatur, Ala.
"You can't love us in Louisville and hate us in Decatur," said Fire.

Facing off against Fire, one of the principle union leaders, is Dennis Rocheleau, a vetran labor relations expert at GE who has been involved in the last nine rounds of contract talks, and was chief neogtiator at the last one.
A GE spokesman said that he had met with Fire, newly-installed IUE president, even before the talks began.

Whether any goodwill will result from those early meetings won't be known for sure howver, until the last week in June. Traditonally GE's labor talks go down to the last minute, say both sides, and this time around it's expected to be no different.
